decision.explanation: Multiplying the first integral by 5 gives ∫₆³ f(x) dx = -5. Reversing the limits gives ∫₃⁶ f(x) dx = 5. Therefore ∫₀⁶ f(x) dx = 3 + 5 = 8.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\int }_{6}^{3}\frac{1}{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-1$ and ${\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=3.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x?$
after.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{3}\frac{1}{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ \frac{1}{5}{\int }_{6}^{3}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ -\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ {\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3+5 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Reversing the limits gives ∫₁³ f(x) dx = 4. By linearity, ∫₁³ (7f(x)+2) dx = 7(4)+2(3−1) = 32.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{3}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(7f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & =7{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7(4)+2\cdot x\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =28+2(3-1) \\  & =28+4 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Reversing the limits gives ∫₋₁¹ f(x) dx = 1. Since 6x is odd, its integral over [−1,1] is zero. Thus the requested integral is 1 − 0 = 1.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{1}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(x)-6x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x-6{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1-6\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =1-3({1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =1-3\cdot 0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
content.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{1}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(x)-6x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x-6{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1-6\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =1-3({1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =1-3\cdot 0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that ${\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1,$ then what is ${\int }_{-1}^{3}(2f(x)-3)\,\text{d}x?$
after.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2+1 & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 3 & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{3}(2f(x)-3)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{-1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{-1}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot 3-3\cdot x\,{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2\cdot 3-3(3-(-1)) \\  & =6-3(4) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$
